notes:
I've written notes on all 16 verses below, followed by a section on where the traditions differ and a list of what I couldn't find. The main finding is that the commentators don't split by denomination on this chapter. They split over whether Elihu is mostly right or whether he misjudges Job.

# Job 35: research notes

## Overview
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Elihu twists what Job actually said and claims God is too far away to be affected by people. He then takes God's silence as proof that Job is ungodly.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Verses 1–8 answer Job's complaint that his righteousness brought no blessing. Verses 9–14 explain that his prayers went unanswered because they lacked faith and humility. Verses 15–16 condemn his arrogance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Gill pictures Elihu pausing to see whether Job would reply. When Job stayed silent, Elihu moved on to other things Job had said. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm
- Benson thinks Job may have kept quiet because he saw that Elihu meant well, even though Elihu read his words harshly.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-35.html

**v. 2**
- Pulpit stresses that Job never said this. Elihu pushes Job's rash phrases to their most extreme logical conclusions.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- **Translation:** Clarke says the line would be blasphemy, but Job never said it, directly or by implication. He prefers the reading "I am righteous before God."  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-35.html The BSB footnote gives the same alternative.  https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/job/35.htm
- Matthew Henry restates the charge in plain terms: Job is in effect claiming he has done more for God than God has done for him.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-1.html
- Gill says the charge must be about the justice of Job's *cause*, not his personal righteousness. Job never said this outright, but his speeches invited the conclusion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm
- Guzik: Elihu misses Job's point. Job wanted to be vindicated precisely because he believed God is just.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: Job argued that his righteousness brought him no *earthly* advantage, but he always believed it would pay off in the end. Elihu ignores that.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Guzik: Elihu accuses Job of cold calculation, as if Job denied that God's moral order means anything.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/
- Gill: our own righteousness does nothing to justify us before God. It still has real value: a good conscience, a good reputation, and evidence that our faith is genuine. Gill also lists other ways the Hebrew can be read, such as "by atonement" or "by punishment." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm

**v. 4**
- Gill: "your friends" does not mean the three friends, who sided with Elihu. It means anyone who thinks the way Job does. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm
- Pulpit takes it to mean the three friends. It notes that Elihu mostly just repeats and expands Eliphaz's argument from Job 22:2–3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Guzik: Elihu's ideas are much the same as the friends', yet he sees himself as different.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/

**v. 5**
- Matthew Henry: the heavens are far above us, and God is far above them, so he is beyond the reach of both our sins and our services.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-1.html Wesley's note says the same thing (the page shows it in Spanish).  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-5.html
- Barnes: God is so exalted that human conduct cannot touch his happiness.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/job/35-5.html
- Guzik, quoting Mason: for Elihu the clouds are a wall between heaven and earth, a picture of God's distance.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: sin cannot harm God. God punishes it not because it hurts him but because it is out of tune with his moral order. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Gill qualifies this. Sin really is against God's nature and law, and it dishonours him. But it cannot damage his essential glory, just as an eclipse does not harm the sun. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: everything already belongs to God, so we can only give him what is his. We cannot put him in our debt. It cites Psalm 16:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Gill: when God rewards good works, it is grace, not something he owes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes link the verse to Romans 11:35.  https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/job/35.htm
- **Critique:** Guzik says Elihu traps himself. If God is that far beyond us, why would Job's repentance matter?  He adds, quoting G. Campbell Morgan, that God's love means he cannot be indifferent.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/

**v. 8**
- Clarke: you can hurt or help yourself and other people, but you can neither hurt nor help God.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-35.html
- Pulpit: Job was wrong to expect God to reward him with prosperity. When God rewards the godly, it comes from his own free goodness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Coffman strongly rejects Elihu's position here.  He points to the cross as the answer to it.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-35.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-1.html

**v. 9**
- Benson: Elihu is starting a new subject here, answering Job's complaint that God did not hear him.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-35.html
- Smick (quoted by Guzik): Job had given whole speeches (chapters 23–24) to God's apparent indifference to the oppressed.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/
- Gill: the oppressed often cry to other people rather than to God. When they do cry to God, it is with complaint or a desire for revenge, not with humility. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm

**v. 10**
- **Main reading:** the oppressed fail to seek God. Barnes:  Matthew Henry: people overlook the mercies they have during affliction, and God is just to reject their prayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/35-10.htm
- **"Songs in the night":**
  - Barnes and Matthew Henry read it as God giving comfort and joy in the darkest times.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-10.html
  - Gill rejects some older ideas: angels' praises (the Targum), the moon and stars, nightingales. He takes it to mean either God's mercies remembered at night, or God's presence in a "night" of affliction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch: God puts songs of praise in sufferers' mouths during their night of sorrow, as help begins to dawn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/35-10.htm
- **Alternative reading (Ellicott):** some render it so that "he who gives songs in the night" is the pleasure-loving oppressor who never asks for God. Ellicott thinks this makes sense and leaves it to the reader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/35-10.htm
- **Older translations differ:**  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-10.html
- **"My Maker":** the Hebrew word is plural. Gill and Poole see a hint of the Trinity in it. Keil & Delitzsch treat it as an intensive plural. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/35-10.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist) applies it to Christians.**  He also reads it doctrinally:  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/job-35.html | https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/35-10.html
- Bible.org says the verse shows God is available to believers even in the night.  https://bible.org/article/singing-songs-night

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: Elihu probably has in mind Job 6:5, where Job compared his complaints to animals' natural cries. Humans have a higher nature and should bring their griefs to God in faith. It cites James 4:3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Pulpit's homily section mentions another reading: God teaches us *through* the animals, such as ravens that cry to him for food (Ps 147:9). Keil & Delitzsch note that most interpreters read the words as a comparison ("more than"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/35-10.htm
- Clarke: animals seem grateful to the hand that feeds them, while people forget God.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-35.html

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: they get no answer because they pray proudly and demand relief as a right rather than asking for it as a favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Guzik: by saying this, Elihu lumps Job in with proud, evil men.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/
- Coffman:  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-35.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: God will not hear prayers made empty by lack of faith or humility. It cites Psalm 66:18 and James 4:3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- The NET translation reads "Surely it is an empty cry—God does not hear it."  https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/35/1/

**v. 14**
- Benson: even if God waits, he will certainly do right by Job.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-35.html
- Pulpit translates "How much less…" and concludes that Job should keep waiting in patience: "the last word is not yet spoken." Pulpit homilist W. F. Adeney says Job's case really was before God, as the prologue shows.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Clarke:  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-35.html

**v. 15**
- **Hard verse to translate.** Pulpit calls the KJV wording "an impossible rendering." It reads instead: because God has not punished Job's angry words or paid much attention to his arrogance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-35.html
- Andersen (quoted by Guzik) admits the verse is obscure.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-35/
- NET takes it as Job's own claim:  https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/job/35/1/

**v. 16**
- Gill: Job did not understand his sins, his afflictions, or God's purpose in them. Job himself later admits this in 42:3.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/job/35-16.html
- Clarke says the line applies just as much to the three friends and to Elihu himself.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-35.html
- Coffman:  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-35.html

## Where the traditions differ
- **Is Elihu right?** This is the real dividing line, and it cuts across denominations:
  - John Wesley (Methodist) explains why God does not rebuke Elihu in 42:7:  https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-job/
  - Bible Hub's study notes (evangelical) agree.  https://biblehub.com/job/35-1.htm
  - Guzik (Enduring Word, from your Pentecostal/charismatic list), Coffman and Clarke (Methodist) are critical of Elihu (see verses 7, 12 and 16).
- **Reformed/Baptist emphases:** Gill uses verses 3 and 7 to make points about imputed righteousness and rewards being grace, not debt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/35.htm Spurgeon reads verse 10 in terms of human inability without grace (see v. 10).

## Other views
- **Catholic (Haydock, on biblehub.com):** Elihu misrepresents ("calumniates") Job. It cites Gregory the Great's view that Elihu's "strong sentences" are ill-applied to "the blessed Job." On verse 8 it cites Augustine: God punishes the harm the sinner does to himself. On verse 10 it lists the Septuagint's "night watches" (taken as the stars) and adds that God's servants have inward joy in affliction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/job/35.htm

## Not found
I found nothing on netbible.org's translators' notes, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org (the Catholic material above came through biblehub.com), on any Lutheran or Anglican-specific source, or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter.
